composing_text: UK-COR-001C (front taken over at noon on 23 July; Stacey: 1st British Corps)
current_activity: Army headquarters becomes operational and takes over the 1st British Corps front
notes: Event date: 23 July 1944, noon (Stacey, p. 196). Event definition: Headquarters First Canadian Army becomes operational at noon, with no Canadian division under its command yet, and takes over the front of I Corps (Stacey: 1st British Corps) east of the Orne. The date follows the official history; the Army was formed in March 1944 and had been in Normandy since June without an operational role (p. 146). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 196: "at noon on 23 July Headquarters First Canadian Army became operational, though as yet it had no Canadian divisions under its command. It took over at that moment the front held by Lieut.-General J. T. Crocker's 1st British Corps"; p. 297: "having moved up from Amblie"; p. 146: "set up his small tactical headquarters in Amblie". Location: Amblie, Calvados with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the headquarters place is the one documented before and after the date, not stated for 23 July itself. Location support: Stacey places the Army tactical headquarters at Amblie from 18 June (p. 146) and says Main Headquarters moved up from Amblie at the end of August (p. 297); it does not name the headquarters place on 23 July. Commander: Gen. H. D. G. Crerar (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 663: 20 Mar. 44 to 30 Jul. 45).

composing_text: CAN-COR-002C (taken under command at noon on 31 July)
current_activity: Takes II Canadian Corps and the front south of Caen under command at noon
notes: Event date: 31 July 1944, noon (Stacey, p. 201). Event definition: First Canadian Army takes II Canadian Corps (Stacey: 2nd Canadian Corps) under its command, and with it the front south of Caen; the corps had served under Second Army until then (p. 200). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 201: "to take under its command General Simonds' 2nd Canadian Corps and with it the front south of Caen"; "finally happened at noon on 31 July". Location: Amblie, Calvados with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the headquarters place is the one documented after the date (the move from Amblie, p. 297), not stated for 31 July. Location support: Stacey names no headquarters place for 31 July; the Army Main Headquarters stood at Amblie until the end of August (p. 297). Commander: Gen. H. D. G. Crerar (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 663: 20 Mar. 44 to 30 Jul. 45).

current_activity: Main Headquarters moves up from Amblie and opens near Brionne at midnight 30-31 August
notes: Event date: 31 August 1944 (midnight of 30-31 August; Stacey, p. 297). Event definition: Main Headquarters First Canadian Army moves from Amblie to a site near Brionne, Eure; the move was delayed by the wish of No. 84 Group R.A.F. to stay near its airfields at Amblie (p. 297, note). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 297: "having moved up from Amblie"; "opened near Brionne at midnight". Location: Brionne, Eure with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the headquarters opened near the town, not in it. Location support: Stacey names Brionne as the place near which the headquarters opened. Commander: Gen. H. D. G. Crerar (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 663: 20 Mar. 44 to 30 Jul. 45).

current_activity: Simonds takes over the Army from Crerar, who is ill; Foulkes takes the corps
notes: Event date: 27 September 1944 (Stacey, p. 373). Event definition: Crerar, suffering from dysentery, hands First Canadian Army to Lt.-Gen. Simonds and leaves for England; Simonds commands the Army through the Battle of the Scheldt and Maj.-Gen. Foulkes takes II Canadian Corps (p. 373). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 373: "Crerar handed over the Army to Simonds and left for England on the morning of 27 September"; "During the Scheldt operations, accordingly, General Simonds commanded First Canadian Army". Location: Antwerp, Belgium with a precision of 50 km. Location approximate: the point is a representative one for the Army area, not a headquarters position. Location support: Stacey does not say where the Army headquarters stood on 27 September; the point is Antwerp, the centre of the Scheldt operations the Army was about to fight. Commander: Lt.-Gen. G. G. Simonds, acting army commander from 27 September to 9 November 1944 (Stacey, pp. 373 and 426).

current_activity: Organized resistance on Walcheren ends; the Battle of the Scheldt is over
notes: Event date: 8 November 1944 (Stacey, p. 426). Event definition: Stacey dates the end of the Scheldt fighting by the cessation of organized resistance on Walcheren, after which the Army had three months without major operations until 8 February 1945. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 426: "cessation of organized resistance on Walcheren on 8 November". Location: Walcheren, Zeeland with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the island is represented by the existing area place; the place of the Army headquarters is not given. Location support: Stacey names Walcheren as the last area of resistance (p. 426). Commander: Lt.-Gen. G. G. Simonds, acting army commander from 27 September to 9 November 1944 (Stacey, pp. 373 and 426).

current_activity: Crerar returns and resumes command of the Army at noon; Simonds returns to the corps
notes: Event date: 9 November 1944, noon (Stacey, p. 426). Event definition: Gen. Crerar resumes command of First Canadian Army at noon on 9 November; Simonds returns to II Canadian Corps and Foulkes leaves for Italy; the Army takes control of the Nijmegen bridgehead at the same hour (p. 428). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 426: "returned to Headquarters First Canadian Army on 7 November"; "at noon on the 9th". Location: Antwerp, Belgium with a precision of 50 km. Location approximate: the point is a representative one for the Army area, not a headquarters position. Location support: Stacey does not say where the Army headquarters stood in November; the point is the same representative one as on 27 September. Commander: Gen. H. D. G. Crerar (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 663: 20 Mar. 44 to 30 Jul. 45).

current_activity: Warns corps commanders of a possible German attack on the Army front during the Ardennes offensive
notes: Event date: 23 December 1944 (Stacey, p. 443). Event definition: While the Ardennes offensive is under way, Crerar tells his corps commanders to be on the alert for a subsidiary water and airborne attack on North Brabant and perhaps Antwerp; the Army has been told the 30th Corps cannot yet return and its main task is the defence of the Nijmegen Salient (p. 442). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 442: "the defence of the Nijmegen Salient"; p. 443: "On 23 December General Crerar issued to his Corps Commanders a cautionary directive pointing to the possibility of". Location: Nijmegen, Gelderland with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point stands for the Army front; the Army headquarters place is not given. Location support: Stacey names the Nijmegen Salient as the Army most important responsibility (p. 442); the whole Army front is concerned in the directive. Commander: Gen. H. D. G. Crerar (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 663: 20 Mar. 44 to 30 Jul. 45).
